senses.gloss: To protect a natural place, a species, or an old building from harm or loss.
examples: The trust works to *conserve* wetlands along the coast.
The town *conserved* its old courthouse instead of tearing it down.
Several rare species are being *conserved* in the park.

senses.gloss: Of events or conditions, to seem to combine to produce a bad result.
examples: Bad weather and a flat tire *conspired* to ruin the trip.
Everything seems to *conspire* against us on moving day.
Traffic, rain, and a late train were *conspiring* to make him miss the wedding.

senses.gloss: To work as an outside expert for a company, usually for a fee.
examples: She *consults* for two hospitals in the area.
After he retired, he *consulted* part-time.
He has been *consulting* for startups since 2019.

senses.gloss: To use up fuel, money, time, or other resources.
examples: The old furnace *consumes* a lot of gas.
The project *consumed* most of our budget.
Data centers are *consuming* more electricity every year.

senses.gloss: To destroy something completely, said of fire.
examples: A fire can *consume* a dry forest in hours.
Flames *consumed* the warehouse in twenty minutes.
The old barn was *consumed* by the blaze.

senses.gloss: To fill someone's mind so completely that nothing else matters.
examples: Guilt *consumed* him for years.
She was *consumed* by jealousy.
Work seems to *consume* his whole life.

senses.gloss: To have something inside.
examples: The box *contains* old photographs.
Does this sauce *contain* any dairy?
The report *contained* three serious errors.

senses.gloss: To hold a strong feeling in and not show it.
examples: She could hardly *contain* her excitement.
He *contained* his anger until the guests had left.
The kids were barely *containing* their laughter.

senses.gloss: To claim firmly that something is true, especially in an argument or in court.
examples: The defense *contends* that the evidence was planted.
Critics *contended* that the law was unconstitutional.
He has long *contended* that the test is unfair.

senses.gloss: To go on speaking after a pause.
examples: "And another thing," she *continued*, "we open on Monday."
Please *continue* — I didn't mean to interrupt.
After *continuing* for another minute, he stopped to take questions.

senses.gloss: To become smaller or shorter, or to make something do this.
examples: Metal *contracts* as it cools.
The muscle *contracted* sharply and he dropped the bar.
Her pupils were *contracting* in the bright light.

senses.gloss: To be so different from another fact or statement that both cannot be true.
examples: The new figures *contradict* last year's report.
His second statement *contradicted* the first.
The two witnesses have *contradicted* each other on every detail.

senses.gloss: To be one of the causes of something.
examples: Smoking *contributes* to heart disease.
Poor lighting *contributed* to the accident.
Several factors have *contributed* to the delay.

senses.gloss: To make a machine or a vehicle do what you want.
examples: A single chip *controls* the whole system.
The pilot *controlled* the plane with one hand.
He was *controlling* the drone from the parking lot.

senses.gloss: To hold your own feelings or behavior in check.
examples: Try to *control* your temper.
She *controlled* herself and said nothing.
He has trouble *controlling* his spending.

senses.gloss: To keep something within safe limits so that it does not get worse.
examples: Diet and exercise can *control* blood pressure.
Firefighters *controlled* the blaze by midnight.
The infection is being *controlled* with antibiotics.

senses.gloss: To change something into a different form or a different use.
examples: They *converted* the garage into a bedroom.
Solar panels *convert* sunlight into electricity.
The old factory is being *converted* into apartments.

senses.gloss: To change your religion, or to make someone else change theirs.
senses.ru: обращать в веру; переходить в другую веру
examples: He *converted* to Judaism before the wedding.
Missionaries tried to *convert* the whole village.
She was *converted* by a book she read in college.

senses.gloss: To become less friendly or less enthusiastic.
examples: Relations between the two countries have *cooled*.
His interest in the project began to *cool* after a month.
With demand *cooling*, the store cut its prices.

senses.gloss: To match well with something else in color or style.
examples: Do these shoes *coordinate* with the dress?
She *coordinated* her tie with her shirt.
The bridesmaids wore *coordinating* dresses.

senses.gloss: To send someone a copy of a message that is mainly for someone else.
examples: Please *copy* me on that email.
She *copied* her manager on the reply.
I've been *copied* on every message in the thread.

senses.gloss: To include or deal with a subject.
examples: The exam will *cover* chapters one through six.
We *covered* that material last week.
That error isn't *covered* in the manual.

senses.gloss: To pay for a loss or a cost, said of insurance or of an amount of money.
examples: Does your policy *cover* flood damage?
Insurance *covered* most of the repair.
Dental work isn't *covered* by this plan.

senses.gloss: To report on an event or a subject as a journalist.
examples: She *covers* the White House for a wire service.
He *covered* the trial for three months.
Dozens of reporters were *covering* the storm.

senses.gloss: To do someone's job while they are away.
examples: Can you *cover* my shift on Friday?
She *covered* the front desk while I was out.
Who's *covering* the phones at lunch?

senses.gloss: To make a sudden sharp sound.
examples: Thunder *cracked* over the lake.
The whip *cracks* like a gunshot.
Branches were *cracking* under his boots.

senses.gloss: To solve something difficult, such as a code or a criminal case.
examples: Detectives finally *cracked* the case.
No one could *crack* the code.
The password has never been *cracked*.

senses.gloss: To lose control of yourself under pressure.
examples: He *cracked* during the second hour of questioning.
Most people would *crack* under that kind of stress.
She was *cracking* under the workload.

senses.gloss: To force too much into a small space.
examples: He *crammed* his clothes into one bag.
Don't *cram* so much into the drawer.
Two hundred people were *crammed* into the hall.

senses.gloss: To stop working suddenly, said of a computer or a program.
examples: My laptop *crashed* and I lost the file.
The app *crashes* every time I open a photo.
The site has *crashed* twice today.

senses.gloss: To fall suddenly and steeply in value.
examples: The market *crashed* in 1929.
Housing prices could *crash* again.
Tech stocks have *crashed* twice this decade.

senses.gloss: To sleep somewhere that is not your own home, usually for one night.
examples: Can I *crash* at your place tonight?
He *crashed* on the couch after the party.
We ended up *crashing* in the car.

senses.gloss: To be completely full of moving people or insects.
examples: The kitchen was *crawling* with ants.
Downtown *crawls* with tourists in July.
The building *crawled* with reporters all week.

senses.gloss: To say publicly that someone is responsible for something good.
examples: She *credits* her mother with teaching her to cook.
He *credited* the win to his teammates.
Fleming is *credited* with discovering penicillin.

senses.gloss: To put one arm or one leg over the other.
examples: Don't *cross* your arms during the interview.
She *crossed* her legs and waited.
He listened with his arms *crossed*.

senses.gloss: To win easily, without being seriously challenged.
examples: They *cruised* to a 5-0 win.
The favorite should *cruise* through the first round.
She is *cruising* toward re-election.

senses.gloss: To fail or fall apart gradually.
examples: The deal *crumbled* at the last minute.
Their defense began to *crumble* in the fourth quarter.
Support for the bill is *crumbling*.

senses.gloss: To work through a large amount of numbers or data.
examples: Let me *crunch* the numbers and get back to you.
She *crunched* the sales data overnight.
The team spent the week *crunching* survey results.

senses.gloss: To defeat someone or something completely.
examples: They *crushed* us 40-0.
Troops were sent in to *crush* the protest.
The rebellion was *crushed* within days.

senses.gloss: To upset someone very badly.
examples: The news *crushed* her.
Losing the scholarship would *crush* him.
He was *crushed* when they turned him down.

senses.gloss: To shout or say something loudly.
examples: "Look out!" he *cried*.
We heard someone *cry* her name.
The fans were *crying* for an encore.

senses.gloss: To become clear and definite, said of ideas or plans.
examples: The plan *crystallized* over dinner.
It took months for his ideas to *crystallize*.
Opposition is *crystallizing* into a real movement.

senses.gloss: To put handcuffs on someone.
examples: The officer *cuffed* him and read him his rights.
They *cuff* everyone before the transport.
He was *cuffed* and put in the back of the car.

senses.gloss: To build a relationship, a skill, or an image deliberately over time.
examples: He *cultivated* contacts at every major paper.
It takes years to *cultivate* that kind of trust.
She has been *cultivating* a reputation for honesty.

senses.gloss: To preserve meat or fish with salt, smoke, or drying.
examples: They *cure* the ham for eighteen months.
The salmon was *cured* in salt and sugar.
He spent the fall *curing* venison.

senses.gloss: To form into a curved or spiral shape, especially of hair.
examples: Her hair *curls* in humid weather.
She *curled* her hair for the wedding.
The leaves were *curling* at the edges.

senses.gloss: To bend in a smooth line instead of running straight.
examples: The road *curves* sharply to the left.
The river *curved* around the hill.
A path *curving* through the trees led to the lake.

senses.gloss: To make a feeling or an effect weaker.
examples: The rain didn't *dampen* their enthusiasm.
Higher rates *dampened* demand for houses.
Bad reviews are *dampening* ticket sales.

senses.gloss: Of a face or a mood, to become angry or unhappy.
examples: His face *darkened* when he heard the name.
Her mood *darkens* every time the subject comes up.
The room went quiet, his expression *darkening*.

senses.gloss: To destroy someone's hopes or plans suddenly.
examples: The injury *dashed* his hopes of playing.
One bad quarter can *dash* a whole year's plan.
Her dreams of law school were *dashed*.

senses.gloss: To go out regularly with someone you are romantically interested in.
examples: They *dated* for two years before getting married.
Is she *dating* anyone right now?
He doesn't *date* much these days.

senses.gloss: To work out how old something is.
examples: Scientists *dated* the bones to 10,000 BC.
Experts can *date* a painting from its pigments.
The wreck has been *dated* to the 1700s.

senses.gloss: To think something over carefully, weighing two choices.
examples: I *debated* whether to call her.
He's still *debating* which offer to take.
Don't *debate* it too long — the sale ends tonight.
